absent: Hyper-V hypercall handling beyond delegation when the high operation bit is set.
Full Xen version, event-channel, scheduler and vCPU operation semantics outside the accelerated subset.
Userspace completion behavior for Xen hypercall exits after the return address snapshot.
Computation of maximum event-channel port and poll mask wakeup paths outside the fragments.
Fast event-channel delivery internals and non-backpressure error handling.
Instruction-skip, privilege-fetch, spin-notify, timer-enable, timer-stop, clock-read and TSC translation helper internals.
Layout of poll, shared-info, compatibility, timer and vCPU Xen structures beyond field usage shown.
Configuration defaults and update paths for halt-poll tunables and per-VM overrides.
Signal, scheduler, timer, tracing and statistics infrastructure beyond call sites shown.

findings.text: Xen hypercall entry examines a high flag in the guest operation number for Hyper-V redirection, otherwise gathers operation number plus six arguments according to guest width, records privilege level and trace data, attempts in-kernel acceleration for a small subset, and otherwise arranges a userspace exit carrying mode, privilege, operation and arguments.

Argument collection depends on guest width: narrow guests use low general registers while wide guests use the 64-bit argument register set. The 64-bit timeout for the timer operation is reconstructed from two narrow parameters when in narrow mode. Non-64-bit builds treat unexpected wide entry as a host bug and I/O error.

Only privilege level zero is eligible for in-kernel acceleration. A higher privilege level bypasses the operation dispatch and goes directly to userspace handling, leaving rare userspace-permitted operations to the virtual machine monitor.
Successful in-kernel handling stores the numeric result into the guest return register and advances guest execution past the emulated hypercall instruction, returning the skip outcome to the caller.

Unhandled operations transition to userspace with exit reason Xen and hypercall subtype, preserving long mode flag, privilege, operation and all six parameters. Host also snapshots the guest linear return address and installs a completion callback for resumption after userspace I/O, then returns zero to indicate an exit was queued.

Scheduler operation dispatch handles poll and yield. Poll is attempted first and on success completes immediately; poll refusal falls through to yield behavior. Yield notifies the spin path and reports success with zero status. All other commands decline handling.

Poll handling requires in-kernel local APIC support and an event-channel send configuration flag, otherwise it declines. It then fetches a guest poll descriptor, using a smaller compatibility layout for narrow guests on 64-bit hosts and the native layout otherwise, translating the narrow pointer before further use.

Polled port count above one uses dynamic allocation while single-port polls use stack storage. Counts above one hundred twenty eight are rejected as invalid. Each listed port is bounds checked against the maximum port for the VM, with violations reported as invalid.

Validated polls publish either the single port or a sentinel for multi-port waits, set the calling vCPU bit in the VM poll mask, and test for already pending events. If none are pending the vCPU moves to halted state, optionally arms a jiffies-based poll timeout, blocks, then disarms the timeout and returns to runnable. Poll state is cleared and the mask bit removed on all completion paths, with dynamic storage released for multi-port waits.

Pending-event test holds the VM sleepable read-side critical section and the shared-info cache read lock with interrupts saved. If the cache is not valid for a page it releases both and reports no decision as pending, otherwise it inspects pending state under the locks before releasing in reverse order.
Pending-event inspection selects the 64-bit or compatibility shared-info layout based on host width support and the VM long-mode flag, then reports whether any requested port has its pending bit set.

vCPU halt entry caps the per-vCPU poll duration against the current maximum, decides whether polling is allowed by architecture state and configured duration, performs an optional busy-poll phase, then performs a blocking wait, updates timing statistics, adaptively revises the poll duration, and emits a wakeup trace with total halt time and wait outcome.

Halt blocking has three phases: bounded spinning while abort checks pass and polling remains permitted, followed by a sleep that may or may not actually schedule out, followed by adaptive adjustment. Invalid wakeups shrink the interval; with a nonzero ceiling, long sleeps shrink it, short halts with headroom grow it, otherwise it is preserved; a zero ceiling disables polling.

Busy polling continues only while a single task is running, no reschedule is pending, and current time precedes the computed stop time. Architecture permission is denied when the low bit of the polling control MSR is clear.

Blocking primitive marks the vCPU as blocking, notifies architecture entry, prepares on the architecture wait object, then loops in interruptible sleep until an abort condition appears. It finalizes the wait, notifies architecture exit, clears the blocking mark, and reports whether a schedule occurred.

Abort checks under read-side protection treat a runnable vCPU, a pending timer, a pending signal, or an unblock request as reasons to stop waiting. Absence of all four allows continued sleep. The same check is used both inside the busy-poll loop and the sleep loop.
Block abort inspection holds the VM sleepable read-side lock across the runnable, timer, signal and request tests, releasing before returning the interrupt versus continue status.

Halt statistics count attempted and successful polls, invalid successful polls, accumulated wait time, success versus failure poll durations, and log-histogram samples of wait and poll durations. Polling is deemed successful when no schedule occurred, even if the wakeup arrived after the spin loop but before sleep completed.

Poll interval growth multiplies the current value by a configurable factor with a configurable floor, doing nothing when growth is disabled, while shrink divides by a configurable divisor or zeroes when the divisor is zero and then zeroes any result below the growth floor. Both paths emit a directional trace with identifiers and old versus new values.

Maximum poll duration comes from the per-VM override when enabled, with an acquire barrier separating the enable flag from the value read, otherwise from a global setting. Values are accessed with one-time read semantics in both paths.

vCPU operation handler accepts only set and stop singleshot timer commands and declines otherwise. It also declines when timer support is disabled for the vCPU or when the calling vCPU has no valid Xen identifier.

Timer operations must target the calling vCPU itself; a different target identifier is rejected as invalid. Set reads a guest timer descriptor whose copy length depends on guest width, preserving compatibility layout checks for offset and field sizes, then starts the timer; stop cancels it. Both report zero on success and fault status when guest memory cannot be read.

Timer start converts a guest absolute kvmclock deadline into a host monotonic deadline. When constant TSC and master-clock use are available it prefers the guest compatibility clock cache and falls back to the secondary time cache, samples monotonic time together with host TSC, translates through the level-one TSC view and paravirtual clock, and otherwise falls back to kvmclock plus monotonic now. It then cancels any prior timer, clears pending state, records expiry, invokes the expiry path immediately when overdue, or arms an absolute hard high-resolution timer.

When requested by the timer operation path, negative absolute deadlines and very large positive deltas characteristic of counter overflow are replaced by a short future delay of one hundred milliseconds rather than the guest-provided value.

Timer restart checks recorded expiry before cancel to avoid racing an already firing timer; false positives from the check are benign. Pending state is cleared before rearming so a concurrent callback cannot be mistaken for the new deadline.

Timer expiry callback recovers the vCPU from the timer object, does nothing further if a deferred delivery is already pending, otherwise attempts fast event-channel delivery on the timer port with two-level priority. Success clears expiry; backpressure defers by recording pending, requesting unblock, and kicking the vCPU. Neither path re-arms the timer.

Guest paravirtual clock fetch holds the cache read lock with interrupts saved, drops it to refresh the mapping when the requested range is not valid, then reacquires and revalidates before copying out the clock data under the lock.
Copied guest clock parameters are accepted only when shift and multiplier match the vCPU architectural clock values; mismatch is rejected as invalid without using the data.

Monotonic plus counter sampling reads global time data under a sequence lock, combining base cycles, virtual counter output and mode, shift and offset to yield nanoseconds and a clock mode. The higher-level helper first and last verifies TSC-based mode and reports failure when unavailable, with a separate non-atomic fallback path when 64-bit or joint sampling is unavailable.

Guest memory access failures during poll descriptor, port array, or timer descriptor reads are converted to fault status with handling claimed, allocation failure to out-of-memory status, oversized or out-of-range port data to invalid status, and cross-vCPU timer targeting to invalid status. Early configuration failures instead decline handling so another layer may act.

Accelerated Xen operations observed are version query gated by a configured version, event-channel send for the send subcommand, scheduler poll and yield, per-vCPU singleshot timer set and stop, and global timer set or stop with zero meaning stop. Unhandled numbers fall through to userspace.

Halt and poll state uses halted versus runnable multiprocessor states, interruptible sleep, an unblock request, timer backpressure indication, two-level event-channel priority, absolute hard timer mode, and poll limits of one port for the fast path versus one hundred twenty eight maximum.
